parts: Lesson 23: Environment and Sustainable Development — Summary

The environment is all the living and non-living things occurring naturally on Earth. It is made up of biotic (living) components — plants, animals, birds, forests — and abiotic (non-living) components — air, water, rocks, the sun. These influence each other.
As more goods are produced, more resources are used up. Factory smoke and sewage pollute air and water, and the destruction of nature harms human, social and economic life.

(1) It provides both renewable and non-renewable resources. Renewable resources, such as forests and fish, are replenished over time. Non-renewable resources, such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and minerals, run out; all current energy sources may be used up within 50–75 years.
(2) It absorbs harmful wastes — smoke, sewage and industrial effluents — and cleans and recycles them through natural processes.
(3) It sustains life through biodiversity, the variety of life forms and their links with the non-living environment.
(4) It has aesthetic value: scenery and landscapes.

Pollution is an undesirable change in the quality of a natural resource or ecosystem that harms living beings. A pollutant is the waste or substance that causes it, such as smoke, dust, poisonous gases, effluents or sewage.

Air pollution comes from harmful chemicals and particles in the air, such as sulphur and nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and metals. Man-made sources: smoke from power plants and factories, vehicle exhaust, farm chemicals and dust, paint and aerosol fumes, and methane from landfills. Natural sources: dust from barren land, methane from cattle, smoke from wildfires, and volcanoes. Effects: breathing difficulty, coughing and wheezing, heart and lung disease, and early death (WHO: 2.4 million deaths a year).

Water pollution is the contamination of lakes, rivers, seas and groundwater. Sources: sewage and sewage-treatment discharge, industrial effluents, farm runoff of pesticides and fertilisers, dirty storm water, heated or radioactive water from power plants, oil spills, and algae. Effects: diseases such as cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea; changes in the water's chemistry (acidity, temperature); and the death of fish and birds, which disturbs the natural food cycle.

Noise pollution is excessive, displeasing noise. Sources: traffic, industry (stone crushing, sawing), construction, and household appliances. Effects: harm to physical and mental health — stress, aggression, hypertension, sleeplessness and hearing loss.

Soil degradation is an undesirable change in soil quality: the soil loses nutrients and humus and becomes unfit for crops. Causes: (1) excessive chemical fertilisers and pesticides, which make the soil acidic, saline and toxic; (2) waterlogging from over-irrigation; (3) overgrazing, which removes plant cover and causes erosion. Effects: lower yields, polluted groundwater, loss of green cover and biodiversity, and desertification.

Habitat degradation is the loss of a habitat's ability to support native life because of human activity. It reduces the carrying capacity of the area, upsets food chains and causes extinctions. Causes: deforestation and timber extraction, turning forest into farmland, urban expansion, soil erosion and desertification, and slash-and-burn farming. Effects: floods, droughts, crop failure, disease, loss of ecosystem services and climate change.

Resource depletion is the exhaustion of raw materials in an area, through farming, fishing and mining. Petroleum, natural gas, coal, uranium and gold are becoming scarce because of over-exploitation and population growth. Agencies that protect the environment include UNEP, EPA, IPCC and India's Ministry of Environment and Forests, as well as NGOs.

The Brundtland Report defines sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs." It is a long-term concept. All its definitions require that we see the world as a whole: smoke from North America affects Asia, and pesticides in Bangladesh harm fish off West Bengal.
We can contribute in three ways:
(1) Resources: find substitutes for non-renewable resources — solar, wind, hydro, tidal power and gobar gas — and use renewable resources judiciously.
(2) Recycling: recycle paper to save trees; reuse rainwater through rainwater harvesting.
(3) Reducing: restrain consumption to basic needs — walk, use the stairs, switch off lights and fans.
